# Sources: annotated bibliography and source map

Exact versions of everything the book cites. Times are UTC. "Retrieved" means our own download;
sha256 is of the bytes we received. Raw copies and the fetch logs are kept outside the
repository, in the run directory `~/Hermes/state/quota/runs/rhbook-architecture-11211200/`
(`sources/FETCH-LOG.txt`, `fetch_lean_parts.log`, `headers/`); nothing listed here is
redistributed with the book. The summaries below are ours; tags follow the README ([Paper] for
the two human-written mathematical sources, cited by page; [Community] for everything reported
by others, cited by link).

This file has two parts. **Part I** (below: the source map and the exact-version tables, first
written 2026-11-21 by run `rhbook-architecture-11211200`) pins the sources the mathematical
chapters cite. **Part II** (at the end: an annotated bibliography in six categories — primary
sources, verification, guides and teaching, errata and disputes, commentary, press — plus sources
surveyed only, added by run `rhbook-sources-11211242`) covers the wider public record and gives the
entry IDs that "The story so far" (`chapters/02-the-story-so-far.md`) cites.

## Source map: what each source contributes

**The Lean archive (Alpöge with Claude).** The primary object of the book: 175,187 Lean 4 files
(Lean v4.33.1, Mathlib v4.33.1) whose top file `src/Main.lean` proves five theorems — Mathlib's
`RiemannHypothesis` and four forms of GRH for Dirichlet L-functions defined in
`src/Statements.lean`. It contains no prose, no license file and no challenge file. Every
[Lean] citation in the book points into it by path and line (Section 1).

**Alpöge's note (`remark.pdf`).** Four pages posted on 2026-11-20 with the links to the archive
(footnote 1, p. 1). It announces the proof, made "working with Claude"; says that the method
also gives GRH and, the author expects, ERH; describes the argument as a descendant of
Stepanov's method in which a chain of theta lifts of length about $\sqrt X$ plays the role of
multiplicity (p. 1); explains why only the Lean code was released, mentioning an informal text
of more than 250,000 pages (p. 2); and lists a dated timeline of the main steps (pp. 3–4). It is
the only human account of the method. Cited as [Paper] with page (Section 2).

**Masullo's draft, *The Music of the Primes*.** A 940-page human-written draft released on
2026-11-20 through Vakil's blog, aiming at GRH for all unitary Hecke characters of all number
fields (p. 6). It builds adelic theta functions and idelic zeta functions (Chapters 2–3),
Schauder bases and Hardy–Sobolev topologies (Chapters 4–9), and a trace formula with a spectral
side (Chapter 10) and a geometric side (Chapter 12), Theorem 12.5.1.1 (p. 519). Chapter 13
(pp. 521–522), where GRH is to be deduced, is still a placeholder; Chapter 14 discusses
multiplicities, function fields and higher rank; Appendices A–E collect background. The
acknowledgements (p. 6) mention known glitches and Brian Conrad's help. Cited as [Paper] with
page (Section 3).

**Vakil's announcement.** Ravi Vakil's blog post of 2026-11-20, which released and hosts
Masullo's PDF. It reports that Conrad has studied the draft closely for months, that his feedback
is being incorporated and that it looks good to him so far, and that the work involves no AI.
[Community] (Section 3).

**The Masullo formalization project (`mccorvie/riemann-masullo`).** A community Lean
formalization of the draft's statements, proceeding in waves through the appendices and
chapters, with an errata log. Its README records that Chapter 13 does not yet state the main
theorem, that doubts about the trace formula raised on the Lean Zulip did not come from the
formalization, that its own last two target statements are reconstructions not yet reviewed, and
(at our 2026-11-22 03:30 UTC recheck, ~3,950 of ~4,700 stated theorems proved) that the printed
proof of Structure Theorem I (`Theorem 5.2.1.1`) in Wave 2 does not work as written. [Community]
(Section 3).

**Sutherland's verification page.** Andrew Sutherland's (MIT) log of machine checks, run with
Claude Code: compilation of every module, the axiom audit, `leanchecker` replay, the independent
kernels nanoda, con-leche (including `--compare`), and con-ron (`--compare`), lean4lean, an
independent bubblewrap-sandboxed `lake build Main` whose exported 61.57 GB proof stream matches
the published export byte-for-byte (`5ea74b91…244e`, added in the 2026-11-22 03:10 UTC update,
with 175,186 of 175,187 `.olean` files identical and the single 38-byte bound-variable race in
`LocModel.olean` isolated), and the status of the single-threaded Lean kernels on the export and
of `lake comparator` (still running as of 2026-11-22 03:10 UTC). The most detailed public record
of what has been checked. [Community] (Section 5).

**The LUMI check (`aapolipponen/rh-lean-check-lumi`).** Aapo Lipponen's independent sandboxed
build on the LUMI supercomputer: all modules compile, the hashes of `Main.olean` and
`Statements.olean` match Sutherland's, an axiom and dependency audit of 292 declarations, and the
count that `riemannHypothesis` uses 146,437 of the 175,187 modules. Its `docs/` form a reader's
guide (pages 01–10 and a glossary) edited from AI review reports, with explicit reading-status
markers and a list of what nobody has read. We use it for navigation and cite its findings as
[Community]; we do not reuse its text (Section 5).

**The Comparator setup (`leanprover-community/riemann-hypothesis`, moved from
`Deicyde/riemann-hypothesis`).** A mirror of the archive prepared for Lean's Comparator: a
challenge file stating the five theorems against Mathlib alone, CI, and verification notes that
review the statements, the dependency pins, the kernel fixes included in Lean v4.33.1, a static
scan and the archive's uses of metaprogramming. Its issue tracker holds build improvements and
readers' maps. No Comparator verdict had been posted at our last check. [Community] (Section 5).

**Mathlib at commit `0df444a`.** The eight Mathlib files whose definitions fix the meaning of the
five statements: `riemannZeta` and `RiemannHypothesis`, Dirichlet characters and conductors,
Dirichlet L-functions and their completions, the functional equations, non-vanishing on
$\Re s\ge1$, and the value assigned to $\zeta(1)$. Cited as [Lean] by path and line
(Section 4).

**Buzzard's Xena post (2026-11-12).** Kevin Buzzard's essay on what it means for a claimed proof
to be "checked in Lean", stressing that the first task is to compare the Lean statement with the
intended theorem. Quoted at the start of Chapter 1. [Community] (Section 5).

***Scientific American* (2026-11-20).** Clara Moskowitz's report on the verification effort,
quoting Sutherland's assessment and Buzzard's remark, made on the Lean community's chat server,
that a successful Comparator run was still awaited. Used only for those two quotations.
[Community] (Section 5).

**Literature.** Davenport's and Iwaniec–Kowalski's books are the analytic background the book
assumes; Stepanov's paper, Bombieri's Bourbaki exposé, Schmidt's monograph, and Hasse–Schmidt's
paper are our references for Stepanov's method and higher derivations (Chapter 6); Jacobi's
treatise, Weil's *Acta Mathematica* memoir, and the papers of Howe, Rallis, Kudla–Rallis, and
Gan–Takeda are our references for theta kernels and the theta correspondence (Chapter 7); Katz's
paper on $p$-adic Eisenstein series, Gillet–Soulé's and Bost's papers on Arakelov slopes,
Chowla–Selberg's and Siegel's papers on period/mass formulas, Ribet's and Hida's papers and
Bellaïche–Chenevier's monograph on Hecke congruence ideals and generalized matrix algebras, and the
papers and monographs of Iwasawa, Ferrero–Washington, Sinnott, Mazur–Wiles, Soulé, Rubin, Kato,
Taylor–Wiles, Clozel–Harris–Taylor, and Thorne are our references for the arithmetic engine of
Chapters 8–11; Harris–Taylor, Henniart, Bushnell–Kutzko, Shin, Caraiani, and Green are our
references for Galois representations, local Langlands, and finite general linear characters in
Chapters 12–13; and Hecke, Artin, Brauer, Tate, Weil, Grothendieck, Selberg, Hooley, Deninger,
Connes, Bombieri's Millennium Problem report, and Meyer are our references for Hecke/Artin
$L$-functions, explicit formulas, nuclear spaces, and idele-class spectral realizations in Part IV
Chapters 14–16 (Section 6).

**Classical comparison.** D. H. Fremlin, *Measure Theory*, Vol. 4, Ch. 41, §412E (p. 12) gives closed inner regularity for semifinite Borel measures on perfectly normal spaces. §412W(b)(i)–(iii) (pp. 18–19) gives the finite-open-cover bracket and the corresponding outer regularity, using a countable sequence of measurable finite-mass opens. The metric cases in the text meet those hypotheses. Vol. 1, Ch. 13, §132C (p. 5) identifies the outer length from half-open covers, and §134Fa (p. 17) reads open enlargement and Borel hulls from interval covers. The book specializes these classical results and follows Mathlib for the disjoint-patch proof. The two chapter PDFs were checked online on 2026-11-28. SHA-256: Ch. 41 `113adf0efee490638ffafced49b237a399b9214e1ea7c979de5f56cacf026ddc`, Ch. 13 `7fd026e980d67c9efbc3c55f5df9d2440768a5509dfb2b3d138fb1002525e76f`. [Chapter 41](https://www1.essex.ac.uk/maths/people/Fremlin/chap41.pdf) · [Chapter 13](https://www1.essex.ac.uk/maths/people/Fremlin/chap13.pdf)

**Formal provenance.** `Measure/Regular.lean` credits Sébastien Gouëzel, Floris van Doorn and Yury Kudryashov. The finite bracket argument and the finite and second-countable instances have their antecedents in the Lean 4 port by Pol_tta and coauthors. Gouëzel's #8251 introduced the explicit `InnerRegularWRT` formulation and extracted the general `OuterRegular.of_restrict` from the spanning-set proof. `HausdorffDistance.lean` credits Gouëzel, and `Typeclasses/Finite.lean`, `Topology/Bases.lean` and `Restrict.lean` credit Johannes Hölzl and Mario Carneiro at file level. The particular box consumer is James Sundstrom's #13968 on Kudryashov's framework. [Port #4101](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/4101) · [Refactor #8251](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/8251) · [Consumer #13968](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/13968)

for the transition from admissible levels to recovery and the divisibility minimum. The direct
inputs for extension by zero and surjectivity on units are [MulChar/Basic.lean:134–192](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474/Mathlib/NumberTheory/MulChar/Basic.lean#L134-L192)
and [ZMod/Units.lean:23–71](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474/Mathlib/Data/ZMod/Units.lean#L23-L71),
retrieved at the same pin on 2026-11-23. The unit-fiber tables are the book’s worked examples.

**Chapter 2, §2.3.2.1.** Archive A2's manifest pins the Mathlib Gamma supply. Loeffler's
proof pairs two Euler quotients and takes the sine-product limit to obtain reflection.
The sine-product file credits David Salwinski, “Euler's Sine Product Formula: An Elementary
Proof,” *College Mathematics Journal* 49 (2018), 126–135. Crossref verifies the bibliographic
record. DLMF supplies the classical exact statements on the Euler integral, poles, half-value,
reflection, and both Euler and Weierstrass formulas. The book adds the explicit error estimates
and classroom examples. [Mathlib attribution](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474/Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Trigonometric/EulerSineProd.lean#L11-L20) · [Salwinski DOI](https://doi.org/10.1080/07468342.2018.1419703)

**Chapter 2, §2.3.2.2.** The Beta–Gamma identity in the pinned Mathlib is Loeffler's `Gamma_mul_Gamma_eq_betaIntegral`, which rests on van Doorn's convolution file: the forward convolution on $(0,\infty)$, its identification with the two-sided convolution of the zero extensions, the slice integrability argument and the Fubini exchange with translation invariance. `Convolution.lean` was fetched from the pinned revision on 2026-11-25 (SHA-256 in the table). DLMF 5.12.1 and 5.12.2 give the classical quotient and the trigonometric form used in the $a=b=1/2$ example; the DLMF page was retrieved on 2026-11-25 (SHA-256 `0a5b637be728bb03c53fcd035059aef105e7aef2aa09d226e72fe1a6d7e19a9f`). The two archive consumers are `src/Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Definitions/Divisors/ChernFormSecondChernClass.lean` and `src/GroundTheory/HeightsAndTheta/Heights/HilbertSamuel/PBetaSum.lean` in archive A2. The book adds the composite Jacobian remark and the sharpness example. [Convolution.lean:944–998](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474/Mathlib/Analysis/Convolution.lean#L944-L998) · [DLMF 5.12](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.12)

**Chapter 2, §2.3.2.3.** The Euler-integral supply in the pinned Mathlib is Loeffler's `Gamma/Basic.lean` (2022): the little-o tail estimate, the real and complex convergence proofs, the integration-by-parts recurrence for the truncated integral, and the recursive definition `GammaAux`/`Gamma` with its index-independence lemma, of which `Gamma_eq_integral` is the $n=0$ case. The tail test `integrable_of_isBigO_exp_neg` is Loeffler's `ExpDecay.lean`, resting on the filter-integrability lemma `LocallyIntegrableOn.integrableOn_of_isBigO_atTop` in `MeasureTheory/Integral/Asymptotics.lean`; the zero-end power lemma `intervalIntegrable_rpow'` is in `SpecialFunctions/Integrability/Basic.lean`; the modulus formula `norm_cpow_eq_rpow_re_of_pos` is in `Pow/Real.lean`. All five files were fetched from the pinned revision on 2026-11-25 (SHA-256 in the table; `Basic.lean` byte-identical to the §2.3.2.1 copy). DLMF 5.2.1 states the Euler integral with the condition $\Re z>0$, 5.4.1 and 5.4.6 the values at $1$ and $1/2$, 5.4.3 the modulus $|\Gamma(1+iy)|^2=\pi y/\sinh(\pi y)$, and 5.5.3 the reflection formula; DLMF §5.2 was retrieved on 2026-11-25 (SHA-256 `55178b5f947c6e20ebf933078bc199e3f743dabd6456745621e407d6aea25dad`). The direct archive consumer is `src/Formalism/PeriodIntegrals/UnitaryGroupMassFormula/ExplicitFormula/LGrowthGamma.lean` in archive A2. The book adds the explicit domination constant, the two hand calculations and the sharpness example $s=it$. [Basic.lean:54–105,248–319](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474/Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Gamma/Basic.lean#L54-L105) · [ExpDecay.lean:31–46](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Integral/ExpDecay.lean#L31-L46) · [DLMF 5.2](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.2) · [DLMF 5.4](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.4)

**Chapter 2, §2.3.2.4.** The two integrability criteria behind §2.3.2.3 are in the pinned Mathlib's `IntervalIntegral/FundThmCalculus.lean` (header: Yury Kudryashov, Patrick Massot, Sébastien Gouëzel, 2020) and `IntegralEqImproper.lean` (header: Anatole Dedecker, Bhavik Mehta, 2021). The first file proves the one-sided fundamental theorem of calculus by a lower semicontinuous majorant from the Vitali–Carathéodory theorem and real induction, citing Rudin's *Real and Complex Analysis*, Theorem 7.21, in its section docstring, and derives from it the bounded-interval criterion `integrableOn_deriv_right_of_nonneg` by a simple-function contradiction. The second file supplies a.e. covers, the passage from truncated integrals to integrability by monotone convergence along a countably generated filter, the half-line criterion `integrableOn_Ioi_deriv_of_nonneg` with its value form, and the converse `tendsto_limUnder_of_hasDerivAt_of_integrableOn_Ioi`; its module docstring gives $\sin x/x$ as the example separating improper and Lebesgue integrals. The two §2.3.2.3 consumers are `intervalIntegrable_rpow'` (`SpecialFunctions/Integrability/Basic.lean`, header: Benjamin Davidson, 2021) and `exp_neg_integrableOn_Ioi` (Loeffler's `ExpDecay.lean`). `FundThmCalculus.lean` was fetched from the pinned revision on 2026-11-25 (SHA-256 in the table); `IntegralEqImproper.lean`, `Integrability/Basic.lean`, `ExpDecay.lean` and `Gamma/Basic.lean` were re-fetched and are byte-identical to the copies listed above. Rudin's Theorems 1.26, 2.25 and 7.21 were checked against a scan of the third edition (1987), Gordon's $x^2\sin(x^{-2})$ example against a copy of the article, and Tao's Proposition 92 and Exercise 94 against the blog page (table below). Archive A2 calls the five interfaces in 57 source files; the two call sites discussed in the text are `src/Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/MeanSquareBounds/GIntegral.lean:21–42` and `src/Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/DedekindLFunctions/LandauTheorems/poleData.lean:91–112`. The book adds the staircase computation, the equivalences for nonnegative derivatives, the hand calculations, the six failure examples and the archive hand checks. [FundThmCalculus.lean:968–1272](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Integral/IntervalIntegral/FundThmCalculus.lean#L968-L1272) · [IntegralEqImproper.lean:89–886](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Integral/IntegralEqImproper.lean#L89-L886) · [Subsection](../chapters/02-functional-equations-and-primitive-characters.md#2324-nonnegative-derivatives-and-improper-integrals-the-integrability-criteria-behind-both-ends-of-eulers-integral)

**Chapter 2, §2.3.2.5.** The Vitali–Carathéodory theorem consumed by the one-sided fundamental theorem is Sébastien Gouëzel's `Bochner/VitaliCaratheodory.lean` (2021, 520 lines, read in full), whose header cites Rudin's *Real and Complex Analysis* "Theorem 2.24"; in the third edition the theorem is 2.25 (p. 56) and 2.24 is Lusin's theorem. Its named inputs are the regularity file `Measure/Regular.lean` (Sébastien Gouëzel, Floris van Doorn, Yury Kudryashov), the lower-integral files `Lebesgue/Basic.lean`, `Lebesgue/Add.lean` and `Lebesgue/Countable.lean` and the simple-function file `Function/SimpleFunc.lean` (Mario Carneiro, Johannes Hölzl), and the semicontinuity files (Sébastien Gouëzel, Antoine Chambert-Loir, Anatole Dedecker, Jireh Loreaux), all fetched from the pinned revision on 2026-11-25 (hashes in the table; `Lebesgue/Basic.lean`, `Lebesgue/Add.lean` and `Bochner/Basic.lean` are byte-identical to copies listed above or in the run evidence). Rudin's Theorem 2.25, Exercise 2.6 and the notes to Chapter 2 (which refer to Saks, *Theory of the Integral*, 2nd ed., 1937, p. 75) were read in the scan listed above; Saks was not consulted. The attribution check for §2.3.2.4, item 4, used the Crossref record of Gordon (2016) (table below): title, author, journal data and the thirteen references (Volterra 1881, Bartle, Bressoud, Bruckner–Bruckner–Thomson, Gordon's monograph, Hawkins, Hobson, Stromberg) were verified; the article text was not accessible, and the earlier wording attributing the $x^2\sin(x^{-2})$ example to it was withdrawn. The book adds the three hand calculations, the Baire argument, the counting-measure example and the envelope remark. [VitaliCaratheodory.lean:92–518](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Integral/Bochner/VitaliCaratheodory.lean#L92-L518) · [Regular.lean:308–359](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Measure/Regular.lean#L308-L359) · [Subsection](../chapters/02-functional-equations-and-primitive-characters.md#2325-the-vitalicarathéodory-majorant-lower-semicontinuous-upper-bounds-for-integrable-functions-and-what-the-one-sided-fundamental-theorem-takes-from-them)

**Chapter 2, §2.3.2.6.** The monotone convergence theorem retained by §2.3.2.4 is Mario Carneiro and Johannes Hölzl's `Lebesgue/Add.lean` (2018), whose docstring names it the Beppo Levi lemma. It is read with the lower-integral definitions in `Lebesgue/Basic.lean` and the decreasing form in `Lebesgue/Sub.lean` (same authors), Rémy Degenne's `Function/AEMeasurableSequence.lean` (2021) for the almost-everywhere representatives, Johannes Hölzl and Mario Carneiro's `Measure/MeasureSpace.lean` and `Measure/Restrict.lean` for continuity from below for arbitrary sets, and Anatole Dedecker and Bhavik Mehta's `IntegralEqImproper.lean` for the covers at both ends. The dominated convergence file (header: Zhouhang Zhou, Yury Kudryashov, Patrick Massot, Louis (Yiyang) Liu) and Sébastien Gouëzel's `EReal/Lemmas.lean` were read for statements only. All were fetched from the pinned revision on 2026-11-24 UTC (hashes in the table). `SimpleFunc.lean`, `IntegralEqImproper.lean`, `Bochner/Basic.lean`, `VitaliCaratheodory.lean`, `Lebesgue/Countable.lean`, `Semicontinuity/Basic.lean` and `Gamma/Basic.lean` were re-fetched and are byte-identical to the copies listed above. Rudin's Definitions 1.16 and 1.23 and Theorems 1.26 and 1.34 were re-read in the scan listed below. Beppo Levi's 1906 note was read at pp. 775–778 in the archive.org scan of the *Rendiconti* volume (table below): §1 defines the integral of an unbounded function as a limit over truncations and relates it to absolute integrability, and §2 states the lemma with a finite limit of integrals and proves it by level-set truncation and the exchange of two monotone limits. The archive call sites were located by a search of A2's `lean/src` for the read declarations (49 lines in 34 files). `src/Development/AutomorphicArithmetic/MeanSquareBounds/GIntegral.lean` (SHA-256 `c0069a447b3899c80e9bb69c884febec55e66b46c169ab9c33ba8603a684fc0d`) was read at lines 66–226. The correction to §2.3.2.5 uses `EReal.continuousAt_add` at `Topology/Instances/EReal/Lemmas.lean:430–444`, whose two hypotheses exclude $(+\infty,-\infty)$ and $(-\infty,+\infty)$ (the audit of §2.3.2.5 cited lines 384–387, which in the pinned file hold the end of a liminf lemma).

**Chapter 2, §2.3.2.7.** The Bochner dominated convergence theorems retained as statements in §§2.3.2.4 and 2.3.2.6 are in `Integral/DominatedConvergence.lean` (header: Zhouhang Zhou, Yury Kudryashov, Patrick Massot, Louis (Yiyang) Liu, 2019). Their proofs specialize `Integral/SetToL1.lean` and `Integral/FinMeasAdditive.lean` (Zhouhang Zhou, Yury Kudryashov, Sébastien Gouëzel, Rémy Degenne, 2021) via `Bochner/Basic.lean` and `Bochner/L1.lean` (same four authors, 2019), reduce countably generated filters to shifted $\mathbb N$-sequences, pass through the continuous linear extension `L1.setToL1`, preserve strong measurability by `aestronglyMeasurable_of_tendsto_ae` in `StronglyMeasurable/AEStronglyMeasurable.lean` and `StronglyMeasurable/Basic.lean` (Rémy Degenne, Sébastien Gouëzel, 2021), and discharge the $L^1$ norm limit in `L1Space/HasFiniteIntegral.lean` and `L1Space/Integrable.lean` (Zhouhang Zhou, 2019) together with `Lebesgue/DominatedConvergence.lean` (Mario Carneiro, Johannes Hölzl, 2018), whose upper half `limsup_lintegral_le` calls `lintegral_iInf` (§2.3.2.6) on decreasing tail suprema. Parametric differentiation under local uniform domination is read in Patrick Massot's `Calculus/ParametricIntegral.lean` (2021) and David Loeffler's `Analysis/MellinTransform.lean` (2023) and `Gamma/Deriv.lean` (2022), alongside the Euler-limit consumer in `Gamma/Beta.lean`. All files were fetched from the pinned revision `0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474` on 2026-11-24 UTC (hashes in §4 above; `DominatedConvergence.lean`, `Bochner/Basic.lean`, `L1Space/Integrable.lean`, `Lebesgue/Add.lean`, `Lebesgue/Sub.lean`, `Gamma/Basic.lean` and `Gamma/Beta.lean` are byte-identical to earlier copies). Magazine* 21 (1948), 167–184 and 237–254, is the historical reference.

pp. 1–2, gives a modern lattice proof with two finite subcovers.

**Chapter 14, §14.4.2.2. Textbook contribution.** The section expands
the pinned proof in the circle setting and computes a uniform
geometric-series approximation and the exact distance from a
negative character to the analytic polynomials. It links the
uniform-density result to the existing Poisson uniqueness step.
[Chapter 14](../chapters/14-masullos-trace-formula-route.md#14422-stoneweierstrass-for-the-circle-character-algebra)

credited author of Mathlib's `ContinuousMapDense.lean` (2021). The bodies of
`exists_continuous_eLpNorm_sub_le_of_closed`,
`MemLp.exists_boundedContinuous_eLpNorm_sub_le`,
`Lp.boundedContinuousFunction_dense`, `BoundedContinuousFunction.toLp_denseRange`
and `ContinuousMap.toLp_denseRange`, together with Zhouhang Zhou's
`MemLp.induction_dense` in `SimpleFuncDenseLp.lean`, Rémy Degenne's
`exists_eLpNorm_indicator_le` in `LpSpace/Indicator.lean`, and the regularity
classes and two approximation lemmas of Sébastien Gouëzel's
`Measure/Regular.lean`, were read at pin
`0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474` on 2026-11-25 (UTC+9); file
hashes are in the table above. Urysohn's lemma (Yury Kudryashov's
`UrysohnsLemma.lean`), `exists_Lp_half` and simple-function density are
expanded in the following entries. The weakly regular inner approximation
remains a named input.

**Chapter 14, §14.4.2.3. Classical sources.** Terence Tao, *245A, Notes 2: The
Lebesgue integral* (2010), Theorem 15 (approximation of absolutely integrable
functions by simple, step and continuous compactly supported functions) and
Theorem 18 (Lusin's theorem), read online 2026-11-25 (UTC+9) as the classical
statement of Littlewood's second principle; the subsection's good-sets proof
of inner and outer regularity for finite measures on metric spaces is standard
textbook material.
[Tao, 245A Notes 2](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2010/09/19/245a-notes-2-the-lebesgue-integral/)

**Chapter 14, §14.4.2.3. Textbook contribution.** The section expands the
pinned proof that continuous functions are dense in $L^p$, aligns each
hypothesis with the circle, computes the exact $L^2$ error of a continuous
cap on an arc and of a two-step function, and explains why the inequality
$\|f\|_2\le\|f\|_\infty$ alone does not give $L^2$ density.
[Chapter 14](../chapters/14-masullos-trace-formula-route.md#14423-continuous-functions-are-dense-in-l2-of-the-circle)

**Chapter 14, §§14.4.2.3.1, 14.4.2.4 and 14.4.2.5. Community formalization.**

**Classical sources.** Terence Tao, *245A, Notes 2: The Lebesgue integral*
(2010), Theorem 15(1) and (3), gives the scalar Lebesgue $L^1$ cases on
$\mathbb R^d$. The SHA-256
`90e5e4eed50169fe62acdf20d528a4b9d583b51dd4ab2178040c3dd446adc621`
identifies the 2026-11-25 HTML snapshot of the dynamic lecture page.
Paul Urysohn, *Über die Mächtigkeit der zusammenhängenden Mengen*,
*Mathematische Annalen* 94 (1925), pp. 262–295, Appendix III §25,
pp. 290–291, uses nested open sets and a threshold. Emmanuele
DiBenedetto, *Real Analysis* (2002), Ch. I §2, Lemma 2.1, pp. 19–20,
gives the dyadic-neighborhood construction. The cutoff proof follows
the midpoint construction in the pinned Mathlib file.

Andrew V. Sutherland, MIT 18.785 Fall 2021, Lecture 14, §14.1, Definition 14.4 and equation (1), Proposition 14.7 and Definitions 14.8 and 14.10. The real basis and standard Lebesgue normalization give the covolume of the half-open fundamental parallelepiped. Retrieved 2026-11-26, SHA-256 `4e59e33ada17f0c8f74237723236ef738cdf74b215f80f7cf3eecd52de2f8206`. [Author's notes](https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2021fa/LectureNotes14.pdf)

The trace lower bound and scalar theta discussion inherit the same-source preliminary review of §1.2.2.13, with its nonnegative integer radius. Genus covolume, short-basis estimates and arithmetic finiteness steps have separate inputs. The static module-import path from `Main` was located, and the status here is local reading with kernel replay and declaration-level dependence pending.

# Part II. Annotated bibliography by category

*Added 2026-11-21 (run `rhbook-sources-11211242`); status as of 05:57 UTC. Part I above — the source map and the exact-version tables — is unchanged; entries here that Part I already pins point back to it instead of repeating its hashes.*

**Conventions.**

- All times are UTC. "Retrieved" is our own download in this run unless another run is named. Raw copies, API responses and the fetch logs (`FETCH-LOG.tsv`, one line per request: time, HTTP status, bytes, sha256, ETag, Last-Modified, final URL) are kept outside the repository in `~/Hermes/state/quota/runs/rhbook-sources-11211242/` (`raw/`, `research/*/raw/`); nothing listed here is redistributed with the book.
- sha256 is of the bytes we received. Pages with live parts (blogs with comment counts, news sites, GitHub pages, Zulip) return different bytes on every request, so for them the hash only identifies our copy; the version line says which text we read. Pages that refused scripted requests were read in a rendering browser; those have no byte hash, and we say so. "HEAD" means we asked for headers only.
- Internet Archive digests are base32 SHA-1 of the archived payload. Where we write "equals our copy", we computed the same digest from our file.
- Each entry ends with what the source contributes and how much weight it can bear. That judgment is about the source as a record of events; it is not a verdict on the mathematics.
- Entry IDs (A1, V3, …) are cited in "The story so far" (`chapters/02-the-story-so-far.md`). A: primary sources; V: verification; G: guides and teaching; E: errata and disputes; C: commentary; P: press; S: surveyed only.

### Alpöge

<a id="a1"></a>
**A1. Levent Alpöge, four-page note announcing the proof (`remark.pdf`).**

- URL: <https://alpo.ge/remark.pdf>
- Author: Levent Alpöge (the note is unsigned; it is posted on his site and its footnote 1 links the archive).
- Version / date: PDF `CreationDate` 2026-11-20 12:52:48 UTC. First Internet Archive capture 2026-11-20 14:19:58 UTC, digest `M652L7WBO6BAV3OFKUXHFEEP4J767IYF`, which equals our copy: the file has not changed since that capture.

- Contribution and reliability: The only account of the method by its author. Page 1 states the claim ("I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis"), says the method gives GRH and, the author expects, ERH "with more time", and that the arguments are formalized "without assumptions"; it describes the proof as a descendant of Stepanov's method in which a chain of theta lifts of length about $\sqrt X$ plays the role of multiplicity. Page 2 explains the timing ("This all happened for me late Sunday night"; he messaged "Dario" — identified by the press as Anthropic's chief executive Dario Amodei — about announcing) and why only Lean was released; its footnote 2 says the informal text "hit 250,000+ pages". Pages 3–4 give a dated list of twenty steps from 2026-10-06 to "11/16/26: GRH", which the note says Claude compiled. Authoritative for what the author claims and when; it contains no proofs, and the author himself warns that parts of the timeline paraphrase an AI summary and may need correcting. Cited as [Paper] by page.

It says nothing about his present position, which the press reports inconsistently (P7, P12, P17 citing LinkedIn, and P21 call him a postdoctoral researcher at Stanford; A4, p. 6, speaks of arrangements "for me to return to Stanford for a year").

<a id="e9"></a>
**E9. Our reproduction of the p. 451 gap (not in the repository).**

- URL: run `rheval-opportunity-11211046`, `work/masullo/NOTE-mbasis-gap.md` and `verify_mbasis.py` (outside the repository)
- Author: This project (run `rheval-opportunity-11211046`, 2026-11-21).
- Version / date: Note written 2026-11-21 about 03:38 UTC; computation `verify_mbasis.py` (CPU 25.2 s). An independent audit of that run was in progress at 05:45 UTC.
- Retrieved: Local files; not published
- Contribution and reliability: [Checked]: for $F=\mathbb Q$, $\chi=1$, the norm formula of Prop. 10.2.1.3 (p. 443) gives $\|\eta_t\|\cdot\|\psi_t\|\ge (J_s/Q_s(d))^{1/2}$ for two critical zeros at distance $d$, which is about $1/d$ for $s=4$; since zeros with $d\to0$ exist (Conrey 1989 plus zero counting), no uniform constant exists. A ball-arithmetic computation of Hardy's $Z$ finds sign changes isolating two zeros (nos. 6709 and 6710, about 0.0377 apart) in an interval of length 0.0497, which forces $\|\eta_t\|\,\|\psi_t\|\ge 20.4565$ for $s=4$. Priority belongs to others (E6, E2); our note had credited E2 and is corrected here. A same-project check, not yet independently audited.

**Classical sources checked 28 November 2026.**

- Paul Erdős, *Some applications of probability to graph theory and combinatorial problems* (1964), §3, pp. 134–135, credits Tibor Szele's first-moment count of Hamiltonian paths. It supplies the first-moment precedent. The conditioned orbit counts and host-scale constants come from A2. PDF SHA-256 `e6060ea331d2b26d87a041d25acc13c64bce5e750cc3012c076b6e9c9ee575fc`. - Pafnuty Chebyshev, *Mémoire sur les nombres premiers*, *J. Math. Pures Appl.* 17 (1852), pp. 366–390, at pp. 369–370 uses factorial identities to compare coefficients of $\log p$ and account for prime powers. The modern filtered relative estimate, with its signed main term and scale, uses the A2 specialization and the named analytic inputs. PDF SHA-256 `cb1534bcfbf7a2356af67532592ffa917ac8b5db7bf5c59b64a14af3476db796`. [Original article](https://www.numdam.org/item/JMPA_1852_1_17__366_0.pdf#page=5)
- J. S. Milne, *Class Field Theory*, v4.03 (2020), V §1, pp. 149–150, Definition 1.3, Proposition 1.6 and Theorem 1.7 give the modulus, integral two-multiplier relation and finite ray-group exact sequence. The imaginary quadratic application has an empty infinite part. PDF SHA-256 `50d79af78250a9f1117ad9d337e0b231704a533fc707966ed1bfa52e13d498f5`. [Author's notes](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/CFT.pdf)
- Asif Zaman, *Explicit estimates for the zeros of Hecke L-functions*, arXiv:1502.05679v4, pp. 2–3, Theorem 1.1 and the remark after Corollary 1.2 are precedent for at most one simple real exceptional zero of a real character, allowing the principal character, in the stated rectangle at bounded height for sufficiently large field and modulus parameter. §2.1 distinguishes the common modulus from the inducing conductor. The region and uniform endpoint estimates used here come from the A2 inputs under §§17.4.10–14. PDF SHA-256 `ca1ab8d8844994b999f99d7a97dfa0ae4770a8f8687f07886e81946f94d25941`. **Classical sources.** Hardy and Riesz, *The General Theory of Dirichlet's Series* (1915), Ch. I, Theorems 2–4 (pp. 3–5) and 8 (p. 8) distinguish interior convergence and differentiation for ordered series from absolute convergence. Montgomery and Vaughan, *Multiplicative Number Theory I* (2007), §1.2, Theorem 1.1, Corollary 1.2 and (1.8) on pp. 11–13 give the interior uniform convergence and derivative of the ordered sum. DLMF (25.2.6) records the zeta derivative for $\Re s>1$, and (25.15.1) the defining Dirichlet character series for $\Re s>1$. Runge's polynomial approximation theorem, as stated in Debray's *Complex Analysis* notes, Thm. 6.4, supplies approximation on compact sets with connected complement for the pointwise counterexample. [Hardy–Riesz](https://assets.cambridge.org/97811074/93872/excerpt/9781107493872_excerpt.pdf) · [Montgomery–Vaughan](https://personal.science.psu.edu/rcv4/personal/Publications/MNTI/05.0_pp_1_34_Dirichlet_series_I.pdf) · [DLMF (25.2.6)](https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.2.E6) · [DLMF (25.15.1)](https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.15.E1) · [Debray](https://www.math.purdue.edu/~adebray/lecture_notes/116notes.pdf)

### P13 ideal weight, convolution and real-character square

Archive A2, joined SHA-256 `9631b4f020199e580ba86178cb56c6e9b09f690c2369a80dc4334aa93f49c7fc`. Local R3 covers three previously-named-unread productions feeding `LFam`'s `lam_nonneg`, `lam_le`, `conv` and `sq` fields for the concrete ray-coefficient family of §17.4.15.

`lamRay_props` is proved in `src/Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/GlobalInterpolation/SumLamIdealLe.lean:135–170`. The support, bound and identity-class condition use `pow_prime_norm` (:19–36), `sum_lamIdeal_le` (:38–80), `exists_gen` (:84–111) and `normOne_span` (:113–130) in that file. `ExistsLFamRay.lean:83,102–103,120–123` calls the theorem and installs the fields using the same `D`. The author-level successor corrects the published weight exposition following the earlier partial independent audit.

`aRay_mul_log` (`src/Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/GlobalInterpolation/FiniteIdealsIn.lean:82–134`) proves the divisor convolution identity $a_g(n)\log n=\sum_h\sum_{de=n}\lambda_h(d)a_{g/h}(e)$, using the single-ideal identity `sum_lamIdeal` (`:20–70`, an induction on unique factorization) and a divisor-pair bijection (`Finset.sum_bij`).

`conv_real_char` (`src/Development/AbelianVarietyTheory/Proofs/GlobalInterpolation/ConvRealChar.lean:339–416`) proves the two square inequalities for a real class character $\varepsilon$, using the multiplicative-function machinery `r`, `r_pow`, `r_bounds`, `geom_bounds` (`:19–190`) and the norm-grouping bijection `conv_eq` (`:192–279`), applied to the $\{0,\pm1\}$-valued `chi`.

Hermann Minkowski, *Zur Geometrie der Zahlen*, proceedings of the 1904 Heidelberg congress, pp. 164–173. The planar argument on pp. 164–165 uses a closed centrally symmetric convex region, half-size translates and the area threshold four. Pp. 167–168 extend the argument to higher dimension and give the volume threshold eight in dimension three. Scan consulted 2026-11-25, SHA-256 `4059e4a1319daec3ee10abd2d67528e497f8d061d9504320d7716cfbfca021c5`. [Original proceedings scan](https://jordanbell.info/gs/Minkowski/Minkowski1904.pdf)

J. S. Milne, *Algebraic Number Theory*, v3.08, Theorems 4.3 and 4.19, Lemmas 4.22–4.23 and Propositions 4.26–4.27. These give the ordinary-class theorem, the convex-body theorem, the simplex computation of its volume, and the ideal covolume and small-element bounds. PDF consulted 2026-11-25, SHA-256 `24b83c789a89f25aebffb3cbe4ae5ca29edd0075acc072de093d140770630847`. [Author's notes](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/ANT.pdf)

### Chapter 12 local Lefschetz weight

- **A2.** The local chart proof uses a common Čech representative, evaluates the diagonal pairing on the cotangent exterior powers, compares the two Koszul components, and sums the trace over the reduced fibre. Complete paths and reading levels are in the subsection. [Local Lefschetz weight](../chapters/12-galois-representations-and-local-langlands.md#from-a-finite-étale-chart-to-the-local-lefschetz-weight)
- **Atiyah–Bott I.** Theorem A, pp. 377–378, in the 1967 original gives the simple-fixed-point formula for elliptic complexes with the absolute real determinant. Its Dolbeault specialization explains the complex determinant for a single map. [Original publication](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970694)
- **Serre, GAGA.** No. 12, Théorème 1, p. 19, gives the coherent-cohomology comparison. [Original PDF](https://www.numdam.org/article/AIF_1956__6__1_0.pdf)

Fourier* 6 (1956), 1–42. §2, no. 5, Proposition 2 (p. 8): there is a unique analytic structure on a complex variety for which every algebraic chart, that is, every biregular isomorphism of a Zariski-open set onto a locally closed subset of an affine space, is an analytic isomorphism; the proof rests on Lemma 1 (p. 7: regular maps between such subsets are holomorphic) and uses no implicit function theorem. The Remark after it (pp. 8–9): for these varieties, which are separated, the topology is the coarsest making the regular functions on Zariski-open sets continuous. Page 9: $X^h$ is covered by finitely many chart domains, so it is locally compact and countable at infinity. §1, no. 4 (p. 6): a point of an analytic space is simple when the space is isomorphic to $\mathbb C^n$ near it, equivalently when its local ring is regular; §2, no. 6, Proposition 3 (pp. 9–10): the algebraic and analytic local rings have the same completion. These two, not Proposition 2, are the classical counterpart of the archive's étale charts; Proposition 2 corresponds to the embedding of an affine piece in $\mathbb C^k$. Numdam PDF read on 2026-11-25 and re-read for the corrections the same day, SHA-256 `9898f985dd6932496e26450bfe0beca8655a937032f545b97cebd88d1bc8eb98`. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.5802/aif.59)

### Chapter 1, §1.2.2.3 — Laurent constant at one

- Mathlib at the A2 manifest pin, `0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474`, files retrieved from that commit 2026-11-24 (SHA-256 of each in the run directory). David Loeffler's `EulerMascheroni.lean` defines $\gamma$ as the limit of `harmonic n - log (n+1)` and proves $1/2<\gamma<2/3$. The zeta asymptotics file by David Loeffler and Terence Tao evaluates the Euler-summation error sum at $s=1$ and $s>1$, proves its continuity, obtains the right-real limit $\gamma$ of $\zeta(s)-1/(s-1)$, transfers it to the punctured complex neighborhood, and identifies `riemannZeta 1`. The derivative of the Deligne factor at one is in `GammaDeriv.lean`. [EulerMascheroni.lean:48–172](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474/Mathlib/NumberTheory/Harmonic/EulerMascheroni.lean#L48-L172) · [ZetaAsymp.lean:61–450](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474/Mathlib/NumberTheory/Harmonic/ZetaAsymp.lean#L61-L450) · [GammaDeriv.lean:180–227](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474/Mathlib/NumberTheory/Harmonic/GammaDeriv.lean#L180-L227) · [Fixed proof locations and reading boundary](../notes/proof-map.md#p1-chapter-1-laurent-constant-at-one)
- NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, v1.2.8, retrieved 2026-11-24. The digamma series and Gauss's rational-argument formula give the classical check $-\psi(1/4)=\gamma+3\log 2+\pi/2$ of the quarter-shift Laurent constant; the Stieltjes expansion names $\gamma_0=\gamma$. These are independent comparisons, not formalized in the pinned Mathlib. [DLMF 5.7.6](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.7#E6) · [DLMF 5.4.19](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.4#E19) · [DLMF 5.4.13](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.4#E13) · [DLMF 25.2.4–5](https://dlmf.nist.gov/25.2#E4)

### Chapter 1, §1.2.2.4 — Derivative of Gamma at one half

- Mathlib at the A2 manifest pin, `0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474`, files retrieved from that commit 2026-11-25 (SHA-256 of each in the run directory; `GammaDeriv.lean` byte-identical to the §1.2.2.3 copy). David Loeffler's `GammaDeriv.lean` proves $\Gamma'(n+1)=n!(H_n-\gamma)$ from the log-convexity of $\Gamma$ and the harmonic limit, $\Gamma'(1/2)=-\sqrt\pi(\gamma+2\log2)$ from Legendre's duplication formula, transports both to the complex function and derives the derivatives of the Deligne factors $\Gamma_{\mathbb R}$ and $\Gamma_{\mathbb C}$ at one. The log-convexity (Bohr–Mollerup file), the duplication formula (Beta file) and $\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi$ (Gaussian integral) are used as named inputs. [GammaDeriv.lean:32–228](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474/Mathlib/NumberTheory/Harmonic/GammaDeriv.lean#L32-L228) · [BohrMollerup.lean:111–119](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474/Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Gamma/BohrMollerup.lean#L111-L119) · [Beta.lean:559–601](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474/Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Gamma/Beta.lean#L559-L601) · [Fixed proof locations and reading boundary](../notes/proof-map.md#p1-chapter-1-derivative-of-gamma-at-one-half)
- NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, v1.2.8, retrieved 2026-11-25. The digamma values $\psi(1)=-\gamma$, $\psi(1/2)=-\gamma-2\ln2$, the integer and half-integer formulas, the recurrence $\psi(z+1)=\psi(z)+1/z$ and the duplication formula are the classical comparisons for the hand calculations at $1/2$ and $3/2$; the half-integer formula is not formalized in the pinned Mathlib. ### Chapter 1, §1.2.2.5 — Log-convexity, Bohr–Mollerup and duplication

- Mathlib at the A2 manifest pin, `0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474`, files fetched from that commit on 2026-11-24 UTC (SHA-256 in §4 above; `BohrMollerup.lean` byte-identical to the §1.2.2.4 copy). David Loeffler's `BohrMollerup.lean` (2023) proves the log-convexity of $\Gamma$ by Hölder's inequality on Euler's integral, the Bohr–Mollerup theorem through the logarithmic Gauss quotients `logGammaSeq` and two chord bounds, and the duplication formula for $s>0$ through `doublingGamma`. His `Beta.lean` extends the formula to $\mathbb C$ by the identity theorem, and his `Deligne.lean` rewrites it as $\Gamma_{\mathbb R}(s)\Gamma_{\mathbb R}(s+1)=\Gamma_{\mathbb C}(s)$ for the cosine form of the functional equation. Hölder's inequality for integrals is in `MeanInequalities.lean` (Rémy Degenne) and `Bochner/Basic.lean`; the convexity lemmas are in `Convex/Function.lean` and `Convex/Slope.lean`. [BohrMollerup.lean:58–452](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474/Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Gamma/BohrMollerup.lean#L58-L452) · [Beta.lean:559–601](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474/Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Gamma/Beta.lean#L559-L601) · [Deligne.lean:122–181](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474/Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Gamma/Deligne.lean#L122-L181) · [Fixed proof locations and reading boundary](../notes/proof-map.md#p1-chapter-1-log-convexity-bohrmollerup-and-duplication)
- Alpöge archive A2, joined SHA-256 `9631b4f020199e580ba86178cb56c6e9b09f690c2369a80dc4334aa93f49c7fc`, read from the tarball: `src/Formalism/GammaFactorNonvanishing/RhOfRight.lean` (SHA-256 `7e2c0b519ee420192cad8fb281c2d2bfebae2ba553342fd579c81c2aa0bd3dc5`), whose line 28 calls `riemannZeta_one_sub`, and `src/Development/AutomorphicSpectrum/Proofs/GlobalProofs/DigammaTendstoLogSubHarmonic.lean` (SHA-256 `45b897beaeba6856b67e6862361611be6f30055cdce63c64c58f68ebc3c99a48`), whose lines 8–29 use `Real.BohrMollerup.ge_logGammaSeq` and `Real.convexOn_log_Gamma` directly.
- E. Artin, *The Gamma Function*, translated by Michael Butler (Holt, Rinehart and Winston, New York, 1964), from *Einführung in die Theorie der Gammafunktion* (Hamburger Mathematische Einzelschriften 11, Teubner, Leipzig, 1931). Read in the scan hosted by the nLab (retrieved 2026-11-24T16:58Z, SHA-256 in the classical-source table above). Used: the preface footnote crediting the method to H. Bohr and J. Mollerup, *Lærebog i matematisk Analyse* III (Copenhagen, 1922), pp. 149–164 (p. vi); the non-uniqueness of solutions of the recurrence (p. 13); Theorem 2.1 and its proof (pp. 14–15); log-convexity of integrals by Riemann sums (Theorem 1.9, pp. 9–10); the multiplication formula, its constant and Legendre's case $p=2$ (pp. 22–24). The 1922 text of Bohr and Mollerup was not read. [Internet Archive record](https://archive.org/details/gammafunction0000arti) · [nLab scan](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/Artin-TheGammaFunction.pdf)
- NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, v1.2.8, retrieved 2026-11-24T16:57Z. The Bohr–Mollerup theorem (§5.5(iv)), the duplication formula with its exclusion $2z\notin\{0,-1,-2,\dots\}$ (5.5.5), Gauss's product (5.8.1) and Hölder's inequality for integrals (1.7.5) are the classical statements compared with the text; the total-function form of the duplication formula is Mathlib's. - Keith Conrad, *Finite Fields*, printed pp. 8–11, Theorems 4.1, 4.6 and 5.6. Frobenius order, trace power sum and surjectivity, including the general finite base. [Author PDF](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/galoistheory/finitefields.pdf)

- The Stacks Project, §9.20, Lemma 9.20.7. The purely inseparable degree-$p$ case has zero trace, in contrast to the separable trace criterion. [Original](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BIL)

Classical originals read online 2026-11-25:

- The Stacks Project, Lemma 9.19.1 (Tag 030N), "Primitive element": a finite extension has a primitive element if and only if it has finitely many subextensions, and both hold when the extension is separable. The infinite-base proof avoids finitely many proper subspaces; the finite-base case is referred to Section 9.18. The pinned `exists_primitive_element` carries `@[stacks 030N "The moreover part"]`. [Original](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/030N)
- The Stacks Project, Section 9.18 (Tag 09HY), "Finite fields": the unit group is cyclic, so a generator generates the field over the prime field and over any subfield. The pinned `exists_primitive_element_of_finite_top` carries `@[stacks 09HY "second part"]`. [Original](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09HY)
- J. S. Milne, *Fields and Galois Theory*, v5.10 (September 2022), Proposition 4.19, p. 53 (every extension of finite fields is simple, via the cyclic unit group) and Theorem 5.1 with Remark 5.2, pp. 61–62 (primitive element for $F[\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r]$ with $\alpha_2,\ldots,\alpha_r$ separable; the scalar $c$ avoids the solutions of $\alpha_i+X\beta_j=\alpha+X\beta$; the worked example $\mathbb Q[\sqrt2,\sqrt3]=\mathbb Q[\sqrt2+\sqrt3]$). Same file and hash as **[MilneFT]**. [Author PDF](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf)
- Keith Conrad, *Separability II*, Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 (pp. 1–4), which invoke the primitive element theorem for the trace and nilpotent criteria; consulted for the classical use of the theorem in trace arguments, not for its proof. [Author PDF](https://kconrad.math.uconn.edu/blurbs/galoistheory/separable2.pdf)

The three examples were rechecked by exact arithmetic (`handcalc.py`, SHA-256 `3b4e69beb15eaf08cb5c8d3eada9abd49b874ec9c0fd846193c3ad1813336991`; log SHA-256 `9c46fd5d670a2e408768fd33a10f2dd8a7600aef1f473fa75d7ce041cd25322b`; run directory `rhbook-ch05-quotient-powerbasis-1125g-11250125`, 0.4 s CPU). Classical originals read online 2026-11-25:

- The Stacks Project, Example 9.7.6 (Tag 09G7), "Degree of a simple algebraic extension": the images of $1,t,\ldots,t^{d-1}$ in $k[t]/(P)$ are independent because $P$ has least degree in $(P)$, and they span because each $t^n$ with $n\ge d$ reduces inductively into their span. [Original](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09G7)
- The Stacks Project, Lemma 9.6.8 (Tag 09G1), "Classification of simple extensions", and Lemma 9.9.2 (Tag 09GN): $k[t]/(P)\to k(\alpha)$ is an isomorphism and the degree of the minimal polynomial is $[k(\alpha):k]$. The pinned `adjoinRootEquivAdjoin` and `adjoin.finrank` carry `@[stacks 09G1 "Algebraic case"]` and `@[stacks 09GN]`; the `AdjoinRoot` field instance carries `@[stacks 09FX]` (Example 9.6.4). [Tag 09G1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09G1) · [Tag 09GN](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09GN) · [Tag 09FX](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09FX)
- The Stacks Project, Lemma 9.20.7 (Tag 0BIL): separable, nonzero trace and nondegenerate trace pairing are equivalent; the purely inseparable degree-$p$ case has zero trace; the separable case uses the eigenvalues of multiplication. Same hash as recorded for §5.3.1.8. [Original](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BIL)
- Keith Conrad, *Trace and Norm*, Example 2.4 and the formulas following Definition 2.8, printed pp. 2–3: the matrix of multiplication by $a+b\sqrt[3]{2}+c\sqrt[3]{4}$ in the basis $1,\sqrt[3]{2},\sqrt[3]{4}$, with trace $3a$ and norm $a^3+2b^3+4c^3-6abc$. Proposition 2.34 and Example 2.35 stand under the assumption "We now assume K to be a field of characteristic zero", made on p. 37 at the head of *Finding the ring of integers*; they are cited only for the characteristic-zero Example 1 and for the characteristic-zero case of Theorem 2. The positive-characteristic cases of Theorem 2 (Examples 2 and 3, Remark 2) rest on the textbook proof of §5.3.1.10 and, for fields, on the pinned `det_traceMatrix_ne_zero'`, `discr_powerBasis_eq_prod` and `trace_eq_zero_of_not_isSeparable`, which have no characteristic hypothesis; Proposition 2.26 and Remark 2.28 have none either. Theorem G of the subsection isolates what the pinned proof of `primitive_element_inf_aux` establishes for any scalar satisfying the exclusion condition, with an arbitrary field $E'$ over which $g$ splits; the pinned statement is the existence of $\gamma$. Proposition C (4), that greatest common divisors over $K$ and $L$ differ by a nonzero constant and that the monic one maps to the monic one, is a textbook consequence of `gcd_map` and `gcd_eq_gcd_ab` and of Milne's Proposition 2.17, not a pinned declaration. The calculations were rechecked by exact arithmetic with an implementation of Mathlib's `divModByMonicAux`, `%`, `EuclideanDomain.gcd` and `xgcdAux` over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$ and over $\mathbb F_2(t)(\alpha,\beta)$, and a symbolic check of the purely inseparable example (`handcalc.py`, SHA-256 `6ac4da1582320daf2eda771d223c289843c6265c7f256bc891b0768e33dc03ce`; log SHA-256 `740b92d4c578cdd21955f5596cb3838ea9b219bba0ad0005060120889cefc3fd`; run directory `rhbook-ch05-separable-gcd-1125n-11250255`; 68 checks, 0.2 s CPU). In archive A2, a word-boundary search of `lean/src` finds `gcd_map` in 1 file, `EuclideanDomain.gcd_eq_gcd_ab` in 2, `isCoprime_map` in 1 and `separable_gcd_right`, `eval_gcd_eq_zero` and `primitive_element_inf_aux` in none; these call sites are counted, not read, and lie off the P6 path.

Classical originals read online 2026-11-25:

- J. S. Milne, *Fields and Galois Theory*, v5.10 (September 2022): 1.8 (Euclid's algorithm with $af+bg=\gcd(f,g)$), printed pp. 10–11; Proposition 2.17 (a greatest common divisor computed in $F[X]$ is also one in $\Omega[X]$; proof by divisibility one way and the Bézout identity the other), p. 31; Lemma 2.19, Propositions 2.20–2.21 and Definition 2.22 (a root is multiple exactly when it is a root of $f'$; $\gcd(f,f')=1$ exactly when $f$ has only simple roots; a separable polynomial is one with these properties), pp. 32–33; Remark 3.15 (a finite extension generated by separable elements is separable), p. 39; Theorem 5.1 (primitive element, with the step $\gcd(g(X),f(\gamma-cX))=X-\beta$ computed in $L[X]$ and transferred to $F[\gamma][X]$ by Proposition 2.17), pp. 61–62. None of these carries a characteristic hypothesis. Same file and hash as **[MilneFT]**. [Author PDF](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf)
- The Stacks Project, Definition 9.12.2 (Tag 09H1): an irreducible polynomial is separable if it is relatively prime to its derivative; the pinned `Polynomial.Separable` carries `@[stacks 09H1 "first part"]` and applies the same condition to every polynomial. [Original](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09H1)
- The Stacks Project, Lemma 9.12.4 (Tag 09H3): an irreducible polynomial is separable if and only if it has pairwise distinct roots in an algebraic closure; the proof uses that $(x-\alpha)^2\mid P$ makes $\alpha$ a root of $P'$. Lemma 9.12.1 (Tag 09H0) gives the dichotomy $\gcd(P,P')=1$ or $P'=0$ for irreducible $P$. [Tag 09H3](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09H3) · [Tag 09H0](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09H0)
- The Stacks Project, Lemma 9.19.1 (Tag 030N), consulted again for the contrast with the subspace-avoidance proof; same hash as recorded for §5.3.1.9. [Original](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/030N)

### Chapter 7 §7.4.3.4 — Bruhat filtration

- **I. N. Bernstein and A. V. Zelevinsky**, *Induced representations of reductive p-adic groups I*, Ann. Sci. Éc. Norm. Sup. (4) 10 (1977), no. 4, 441–472, DOI 10.24033/asens.1333. ### Chapter 7 §7.4.3.6 — Cell constituents and extended multiplicities

- **I. N. Bernstein and A. V. Zelevinsky**, *Induced representations of reductive p-adic groups I*, Ann. Sci. Éc. Norm. Sup. (4) 10 (1977), no. 4, 441–472, DOI 10.24033/asens.1333. ### Chapter 17 radial Haar measure and the Gamma factor

[§17.4.25](../chapters/17-behrends-sphere-lemma-and-host-geometry.md#17425-radial-haar-measure-and-the-gamma-factor-in-minkowski-volume) reads the boundary and coordinate-integral suppliers at Mathlib pin `0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474`, fixed by the Alpöge–Claude archive (SHA-256 `9631b4f020199e580ba86178cb56c6e9b09f690c2369a80dc4334aa93f49c7fc`). The integration declarations belong to `Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Integral/Gamma.lean`, which imports `Analysis/SpecialFunctions/PolarCoord.lean` and `Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Gamma/Basic.lean`.

| Declaration and pinned lines | Supply or consumer |
|---|---|
| `MeasureTheory.measure_le_eq_lt` (113–142) | Local R3. Gives the gauge to a copy of the space and uses a continuous linear equivalence to transport Haar measure, then compares the two ball preimages. The statement requires a nontrivial space. [VolumeOfBalls.lean](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Measure/Lebesgue/VolumeOfBalls.lean#L113-L142) |
| `map_addHaar_smul` (336–343), `addHaar_preimage_smul` (352–358), `addHaar_smul` (362–375), ball formulas (418–513), `addHaar_sphere_of_ne_zero` and `addHaar_sphere` (519–530) | Local R3. Scalar determinants give the ball volumes, and left approximation at radius one gives equality. The sphere proof subtracts finite measures or uses singleton nullity at zero. The Haar transport and singleton instance are at 893–903 and 924–944. [EqHaar.lean](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Measure/Lebesgue/EqHaar.lean#L418-L530) · [Group/Measure.lean](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Group/Measure.lean#L893-L944) |
| `integral_rpow_mul_exp_neg_rpow`, `integral_rpow_mul_exp_neg_mul_rpow`, `integral_exp_neg_rpow`, `integral_exp_neg_mul_rpow` (25–73) | Local R3. Real half-line integrals use $p>0$ and, with a weight, $q>-1$. The scaled formula requires $b>0$. The unscaled exponential is the weight-zero case. [Gamma.lean](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Integral/Gamma.lean#L25-L73) |

**Classical sources.** Euler's *De progressionibus transcendentibus* (E19), §§14–15, original pp. 46–47, uses the factorial interpolant $\int_0^1(-\log x)^u\,dx$ and discusses fractional indices. The substitution $x=e^{-t}$ gives the modern positive-real Gamma integral at $1+u$ for $u>-1$. The convergence range here follows from Euler's integral in DLMF. NIST DLMF formulas 5.2.1 and 5.5.1 give Euler's integral on $\Re z>0$ and its recurrence. Milne, *Algebraic Number Theory*, v3.08, §4.21 and Lemmas 4.22–4.23 give the weighted norm and volume by simplex integration with positive radius, and Proposition 4.26 fixes the shared complex basis $(1,i)$ for the covolume. The exponential-integral route is already in the pinned code. Minkowski's *Zur Geometrie der Zahlen*, pp. 164–165 and 167–168, gives the geometric threshold used downstream. · [Euler, Latin text and Ian Bruce translation](https://www.17centurymaths.com/contents/euler/e019tr.pdf) · [DLMF 5.2.1](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.2.E1) · [DLMF 5.5.1](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.5.E1) · [Milne](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/ANT.pdf) · [Minkowski](https://jordanbell.info/gs/Minkowski/Minkowski1904.pdf)

**Evidence.** The radius pushforward and Tonelli proof is an author-level textbook proof for $p,b>0$. Local R3 records the pinned bodies listed here. The deeper sphere-product construction, general Jacobian and matrix determinant proof retain their named scopes. Kernel replay, Main reachability, same-source review, distinct-source review and peer review are pending for this addition. The earlier mixed-volume and class-bound proof retains its own review status.

### Chapter 19 §19.3.18 Cyclotomic irreducibility and the primitive root's minimal polynomial

- **Richard Dedekind**, *Beweis für die Irreductibilität der Kreistheilungs-Gleichungen*, J. Reine Angew. Math. 54 (1857), 27–30. In §§1–3 he chooses the integral monic factor containing the primitive root, compares its reduction with the factor for a prime power of the root at a prime away from the order, and rules out a repeated factor by the derivative. The paper credits Kronecker's 1854 theorem and Schönemann's congruence. The collected reprint, pp. 68–71, was retrieved 2026-11-27 with SHA-256 `9cab339114f71b68fc3e90135f1bb25367eeefc01c3f95f2b1a25484ade8ef19`. [Original text](https://rcin.org.pl/Content/136330) · [Journal record](https://geodesic.mathdoc.fr/item/JRAM_1857__54_147687/)
- **J. S. Milne**, *Fields and Galois Theory*, v5.10, Propositions 1.13–1.14 (p. 12), Lemma 5.9 and Theorem 5.10 (pp. 65–66). Gauss's lemma brings monic rational factors of a monic integer polynomial into the integers. The general irreducibility proof uses $p$ away from the positive order. Lemma 5.9 retains irreducibility as a condition in other coefficient fields. PDF retrieved 2026-11-26, SHA-256 `5c43ea0bf4ec190b819727fe720414a80e09f9e762533d08bad5b8a0b6de7273`. [Author's text](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf)

In Brasca's `Roots.lean` the degree bound yields the identification before cyclotomic irreducibility. Stacks Lemma 10.143.4 gives the finite separable product decomposition for commutative étale algebras over a field. The textbook derives the unit norm image from the resulting real and complex blocks and follows the same tensor witness through the archive maps. **Original sources and assumptions.**

- Anthony W. Knapp, *Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction*, 2nd ed., Proposition 1.143, pp. 116–117, gives the global polar homeomorphism for a closed real algebraic matrix group stable under adjoints. The relation defining the unitary group meets these assumptions. The matrix logarithm gives the smooth inverse used here. Theorem 8.36 and (8.37), p. 538, give compatible quotient integration when the modular functions agree on the closed subgroup. The scalar center is compact, so both restrictions are trivial. The original formula is for continuous compactly supported functions, and equality of the Radon measures extends it to nonnegative Borel integrands. Author PDF SHA-256 `bd7e983a2389349ba5b5e95fdd8b46789b8bc26f9602b3efa20e9c0f80762332`. [Author PDF](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~aknapp/download/Beyond2-clickable.pdf)
- Harish-Chandra, *Discrete series for semisimple Lie groups II*, Acta Math. 116 (1966), 1–111, §37 and Theorem 16, for the discrete-series context. DOI and metadata rechecked on 2026-11-28. The former repository link is superseded by the DOI. [Publisher record](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02392813)
- M. F. Atiyah and W. Schmid, *A geometric construction of the discrete series for semisimple Lie groups*, Invent. Math. 42 (1977), 1–62, (8.1), p. 41, with proof through p. 47, gives the full positive-root formal degree for a nonsingular parameter in the shifted character lattice of a compact Cartan in the connected semisimple finite-center case. For the numerical comparison on the unitary group one uses the determinant-one group and the compact scalar center. The archive's parameter and model identification is a named hypothesis. PDF SHA-256 `6aeed6b336b91ec8606c41d0c544f614fbb027768043fc10e6e9ad9b43317a2f`. [Original paper](https://www.math.utah.edu/~ptrapa/math-library/schmid/atiyah-schmid.pdf)
- Andrew Knightly and Charles Li, *On the distribution of Satake parameters for Siegel modular forms*, Doc. Math. 24 (2019), 677–747, §A.6, p. 736, Remark (1), uses the common Haar numerical formula for the symplectic case, citing Harish-Chandra (1956), §10. PDF SHA-256 `05eadb6c60649277f353327518a6893395b2b09416a7ee1acd6863f1416a6481`. The three PDFs above were retrieved and the cited passages read on 2026-11-28. Anthony W. Knapp, *Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction*, 2nd ed., printed p. 323, Theorem 5.84. Finite-dimensional irreducibility and a highest weight for the semisimple differential give the Weyl dimension quotient. For the two compact blocks the centers act by scalars, removing the trace preserves the root differences, and empty or size-one blocks contribute 1. Per Alexandersson's catalog records the classical dual Pieri rule in partition notation. A common determinant twist gives the vertical-strip correspondence on each block. [Knapp author edition](https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~aknapp/download/Beyond2-clickable.pdf) · [Dual Pieri rule](https://www.symmetricfunctions.com/schur.htm#schurPieriRule)

Keith Conrad, *Exterior Powers*, Theorem 4.2, printed pp. 11–12. The free module is the complex mode space with its ordered pair basis. The classical wedge basis gives the homogeneous support and the inclusion used by `line_deg`. The signed occupation and weight calculation is the A2 argument. PRV's 1966 announcement, §§1–2 and p. 524, gives the diagonal tensor-product result for two dominant integral labels of a complex semisimple Lie algebra and identifies the dual weight by the longest Weyl element. The 1967 journal page supplies bibliographic metadata. Kumar, *Tensor Product Decomposition*, §5, distinguishes the original longest-element result from the general Weyl-element version. The local algebraic matrix statement, real central shifts and signed Fock application belong to A2. [1966 announcement](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9904-1966-11528-8) · [1967 paper](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/1967/85-3/p03) · [Kumar, §5](https://kumar.math.unc.edu/papers/kumar60.pdf#page=8)

Parthasarathy, *Dirac operator and the discrete series*, Annals of Mathematics 96 (1972), 1–30, Proposition 3.1 and its proof, pp. 13–14, use equivariant twisted spinors over $G/K$. This is the precedent for the negative ambient Casimir and the scalar from the compact highest weight. A2 gives the signed exterior-algebra realization, the factor of two, the precise weights and the positive coefficient form on the algebraic tensor product. #### Primary literature

The PDFs were checked online on 2026-11-26. The [slope source register](#acris-gauss-slope-source) gives the earlier page references for the comparison with de Rham periods.

- Jean-Marc Fontaine, *Le corps des périodes p-adiques*, Astérisque 223 (1994), Exposé II, §2.2.2, pp. 76–77, constructs the completed divided-power envelope. §2.3, pp. 77–78, specializes it to the crystalline rings. PDF SHA-256 `74b6bfbaa3a5b5a1eb1f1cd33b0e49aaffa5bde1b8761a91f7cb51a550e9a46e`. [Original scan](https://www.numdam.org/item/AST_1994__223__59_0.pdf)
- Olivier Brinon and Brian Conrad, *CMI Summer School Notes on p-adic Hodge Theory*, preliminary version, §9.1, (9.1.1)–(9.1.2), pp. 128–129. They describe the concrete subalgebra and the agreement of the quotients before and after completion at each prime power. Proposition 9.1.1 concerns flatness and the domain property. PDF SHA-256 `f27d508bc64b3c9e2e9de5041429b2cb6a909b2cd72ff8096c20493f27b5a187`. [Authors' notes](https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/notes.pdf)
- Kiran S. Kedlaya, *Nonarchimedean geometry of Witt vectors*, arXiv:1004.0466v5, Lemma 4.1, pp. 19–21. The Witt Gauss formula at prime weight $p^{-1}$ and its multiplicative seminorm laws provide the classical comparison. PDF SHA-256 `b6408a3e6e55ff6051e18c3d7b1f49e9986a54e02d674c7dbbaa89050c613ede`. [Author preprint](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1004.0466v5)
- Kiran S. Kedlaya and Ruochuan Liu, *Relative p-adic Hodge theory: Foundations*, arXiv:1301.0792v5, Definition 5.1.1 and Proposition 5.1.2(a)–(c), pp. 113–115. That weighted Witt construction has extensions through inversion of the prime and Fréchet completion in the relative Robba setting. PDF SHA-256 `a6a117423db62aec072442bb15b70e3175bcc3b631bdcd6d74f740e3c6cfd942`. [Authors' preprint](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1301.0792v5)

The divided-power unit bound, the local extension proof bodies and the ratio wiring here are attributed to Alpöge with Claude in A2. The book contributes the English proofs, the two explicit crystalline computations and the counterexamples. These literature checks establish scope and attribution.

[Textbook section](../chapters/06-stepanovs-method-and-multiplicity.md#acris-gauss-extension)

The scope of these three readings is local to the listed A2 bodies and direct uses. The three same-source preliminary reviews concern the stated hypotheses and consumers. Full model supply, the deeper adic separation and divided-power inputs, and the general period comparisons retain their named reading boundaries. The book remains a living draft with peer review incomplete.

#### Primary sources and assumption attribution

- Jean-Marc Fontaine, *Le corps des périodes p-adiques*, Astérisque 223 (1994), Exposé II, §§2.2.1–2.2.2, pp. 76–77. The base ring $V$ is separated and complete for $(p)$ and Frobenius is surjective modulo $p$. The original construction takes the completed divided-power envelope of the kernel of a Witt surjection and keeps the induced map to $V$. The classical divided-power identity $x^p=p!\gamma_p(x)$ explains the power law used in the argument. The archive instead takes the weaker power law as a record field and uses its own square-zero BFrame construction. PDF SHA-256 `74b6bfbaa3a5b5a1eb1f1cd33b0e49aaffa5bde1b8761a91f7cb51a550e9a46e`. [Original scan](https://www.numdam.org/item/AST_1994__223__59_0.pdf)
- Thomas Zink, *The display of a formal p-divisible group*, Astérisque 278 (2002), Definition 1 and the normal decomposition, pp. 128–129. The introductory base has nilpotent $p$. The submodule $Q=L\oplus I_RT$ and the generation condition for the semilinear $V^{-1}$ give the isomorphism with columns $V^{-1}$ on $L$ and $F$ on $T$. The matrix is invertible in local Witt bases and $F=pV^{-1}$ on $Q$. This is the classical normalized display matrix. To apply the display axiom directly here would require producing a display and identifying its normal basis and linearized columns with this archive's quasi-logarithm data. The local proof instead verifies injectivity over the residue field via the two coordinate implications. PDF SHA-256 `2293c932bb6147a116eab9418b47646b34756d6b946e799d5eb16366c6b8ba69`. [Original scan](https://www.numdam.org/item/AST_2002__278__127_0.pdf)
- Peter Scholze and Jared Weinstein, *Moduli of p-divisible groups*, arXiv:1211.6357, Definition 3.2.3, Lemma 3.2.5 and Remark 3.2.6, pp. 25–26, on the quasi-logarithm from the universal cover and its logarithmic projection. Their base is a topological $\mathbb Z_p$-algebra with a surjection whose kernel is topologically nilpotent and carries divided powers. Proposition 4.1.3, p. 30, gives Fontaine's completed thickening of a semiperfect base and its Frobenius. The map on p. 42 is the map to the untilt for the specified $T^+$. These constructions provide context for the period rings and dual Lie interpretation. The production proof at the specified series basis is from A2. PDF SHA-256 `984411ef6c3d735a713684d4c9251fbad411a40eab33cefed8ab5c8412b09f6d`. [Authors' preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/1211.6357)
- Stacks Project, Lemma 10.19.1. The ambient ring is commutative and $I$ lies in the Jacobson radical exactly when every element of $1+I$ is a unit. Apply the final assertion with $I=\ker\theta$ after the frame power relation and completeness show $I\subseteq\operatorname{Jac}(B)$. This specializes classical unit reflection. The determinant criterion also closes a separate novelty route for the general matrix lifting lemma. HTML SHA-256 `38206e485a246ad3aed490b5717590a24934c23304279e7cd80116965eb8c359`. [Lemma 10.19.1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0AME)

### Chapter 11 finite perfect local cup pairing

- **John Tate.** *Duality theorems in Galois cohomology over number fields*, ICM Stockholm 1962, §§1–2, Theorem 2.1, Stanford scan at pp. 288–289. Specializing to the constant module of order $n$ gives the two local adjoints after identifying the $n$-torsion of $\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ with $\mathbb Z/n$. SHA-256 61f99c052fe734da98ef56de080bbd5fbc640973e7c4649e3be423f9d2e2302f. [Primary text](https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/BSDseminar/refs/TateICM.pdf)
- **Jean-Pierre Serre and J. S. Milne.** Serre, *Local Fields*, English first edition, IV §2, Proposition 6, gives the unit quotients. Milne, *Arithmetic Duality Theorems*, 2nd ed., I §2, pp. 26–29, gives the finiteness and duality comparison for order invertible in the field. *Algebraic Number Theory*, v3.08, §7, pp. 119–121, gives Hensel and Newton lifting. *Class Field Theory*, v4.03, I §3, pp. 40, 44 and III §3, pp. 109–110, gives the local sign and cyclotomic calculation. Online copies checked 2026-11-26. - **I. N. Bernstein and A. V. Zelevinsky.** The transitivity rule in *Induced representations of reductive p-adic groups I* §1.9(c), with the relation quotient and normalization of §1.8(b) and the mirabolic and derivative conventions of §§3.1–3.5, covers the smooth comparison taught here. DOI 10.24033/asens.1333. PDF retrieved 2026-11-26, SHA-256 `8424600228ab72c5937e45edceefcae410a2a0b8f5ebf282185691542aa89092`. ### Chapter 3 real Lebesgue interval lengths

- **Patrick Billingsley, Constantin Carathéodory, Henri Lebesgue and Terence Tao.** Lebesgue, *Intégrale, longueur, aire*, *Annali di Matematica Pura ed Applicata* (3) **7** (1902), pp. 231–359, defines linear outer measure by countable open-interval covers. Carathéodory, *Über das lineare Maß von Punktmengen — eine Verallgemeinerung des Längenbegriffs*, *Nachr. Ges. Wiss. Göttingen, Math.-Phys. Kl.* (1914), pp. 404–426 ([EuDML 58921](https://eudml.org/doc/58921), HTML SHA-256 `88b84584197a611c6003c0ed50ebd4c1cfdd1a74099a0ec104aaf3729a8595ca`), formulates outer measure on all subsets and the symmetric cut criterion without inner measure. Billingsley, *Probability and Measure*, 3rd ed., Wiley, 1995 (ISBN 0-471-00710-2, PDF SHA-256 `1813e8c52c7424a8f4ee7181e107ff96c789c041650c61a17c29ac36b698fb45`), proves finite peeling and Heine–Borel countable subadditivity on $(a, b]$ in Theorem 1.3 (pp. 12–13), Carathéodory extension from interval semirings in Theorems 11.1 and 11.3 and Example 11.3 (pp. 165–168), and the general right-continuous Stieltjes measure $\mu((a, b]) = F(b) - F(a)$ (specializing to $F(x) = x$ on p. 176) by two right-continuity shifts and Heine–Borel on pp. 175–179 (Theorems 12.4–12.5). Tao, [245A Notes 1: Lebesgue measure](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2010/09/09/245a-notes-1-lebesgue-measure/) (HTML SHA-256 `62e37067d31fc64bb5a51001defb3bf1bd428f663967bfb971ec7ac94bea449d`), Lemmas 6–7 and Exercise 17, gives the box outer-measure recovery and countable almost-disjoint union formulas. Both classical theorems and pinned Mathlib cover the mathematical result in full; no mathematical priority is claimed.

#### First squarefree count contract

For each natural prime $g\ge2^{12}$, each integer $r\ge100$ and each finite set $T$ of polynomials over $\mathbb F_g$, assume every member is monic of degree $r$, squarefree with nonzero constant coefficient, and has distinct roots in the algebraic closure with equal prime-to parts at some prime $\ell\notin BB(r,g)$. The prime and the pair of roots may depend on the label. The real bound is $|T|\le23\log(g)g^{-1/2}g^r$. The proof splits an original pair by equality of minimal polynomials and uses a union bound on the resulting cover of labels. The covers can overlap. The same original family enters `h3` of `counts_of_sqf`. At each host index $k$ and place $v$, `P2` applies `wt_le_count` with $T=S_0$ filtered by `Eii` and $B=23\log(g)g^{-1/2}$, retaining `TieAdmG`, both size guards, $C_L\ge0$ and `lawL`. [Statement, proof and weighted handoff](../chapters/04-auxiliary-prime-pairs-and-host-fields.md#41023-when-prime-to-parts-of-roots-collide)

**Evidence.** The first count has author-level local R3. Independent mathematical review and Lean kernel replay remain open. The original exact-arithmetic certificate checks the two quadratic label sets, the $(4099,100)$ singleton and finite arithmetic checks, with 28,738 passing assertions. Its SHA-256 is `79b7b959e58707dd30e2f2a5a494ed166b273ae9c03a881cf1a035d977d71d9d` (`certificate.json`) and `ccab71229449f316f7bc599453c901e2945ff9def447f1aeedf285589a6f0459` (`verify.py`). `squarefree_div_degree` retains same-source initial review (5/5) for the original third count with $1\le a$ and $2a\le r$. `sqfPrimeFactor_of primes_dyadic_range` retains independent audit for the fourth count with $r/2<p\le r-3$. The dyadic input retains its prior same-source initial review. The `SqfRootShift`, `BBCount`, `ChoiceCount` and `IrreducibilityCriterion` producers have their own scopes, including the latter's separate reading in [§4.11](#chapter-4-411-inertia-lines-and-goodtuple).

**Attribution.** Dickson gives the order, cyclicity, root-count and degree ingredients in *Linear Groups* (1901), §§12–17 (pp. 11–13) and §§23–25 (pp. 15–16). Milne's *Fields and Galois Theory*, v5.10, Proposition 4.20 and Corollary 4.21 (pp. 53–54) give the finite-field, Frobenius and subfield results. Proposition 4.26 and Remark 4.27 (p. 55) give the irreducible-factor and orbit correspondence. Mathlib contributors supply the pinned interfaces for finite-field powers, normal orbits of minimal polynomials, intermediate-field dimensions, monic division, root bounds, prime factors and the logarithm inequality. A2 supplies the specific two-branch estimate. The book supplies the prose derivation and the worked examples. [Dickson](https://archive.org/details/lineargroupswit00dickgoog) · [Milne](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf) · [Contributions](../CONTRIBUTIONS.md#chapter-4-root-collision-exposition)
